title: The SSN in the audit log
spec: M22 · minimize, mask, and log the access not the secret
intro: One risk question, one filing, one clear-text SSN. The answer is correct both times — what changes is whether the number is now sitting in five retained systems you cannot legally empty.

provenance.source: a narrated UCC risk pipeline under a GDPR/SOC2 review; token counts, prices, identifiers and log lines are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: This walks M22's PII Handling and the Audit Trail — minimize, mask, tokenize, then log the access rather than the secret, so an erasure request has one place to go.

steps.title: The risk question, and the whole filing it pulled
narrative: An analyst asks whether ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C. is a high-risk borrower. The pipeline does the obvious thing: it fetches filing 2024-FL-0012345 and drops the record into the window whole — all 41 fields, 3,200 tokens.
The answer comes back correct: five active liens, $2.4M secured, three of them filed in the last eighteen months. Nothing on the receipt looks wrong, and nothing in the output looks wrong either.

But the filing carries the guarantor's SSN, date of birth and home address, and the risk task reads none of them. That is a data minimization failure before it is anything else: regulated data entered the window because nobody drew a line between available and needed.
steps.youDo: List the fields your task actually reads. Every other field in the record is exposure you took on for nothing.

terminal.text: is ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C. high risk? summarize its lien exposure.
assemble_context(filing_id="2024-FL-0012345")
filing block: 41 fields, verbatim · 3,200 tokens
HIGH RISK — 5 active liens, $2.4M secured, 3 filed in the last 18 months.
audit.log <- {"prompt": "... GUARANTOR_SSN: 412-88-7391  DOB: 1974-03-02 ..."}

view.question: is ACME high risk? summarize its lien exposure.
view.verdictNote: the risk answer is right — which is exactly why nobody looked at what else went in

steps.title: One field, five places it now lives
narrative: Trace the SSN forward instead of backward. It entered the prompt, so it reached the model. The model's summary quoted the guarantor line, so it reached the stored report. The stable prefix was cached, so it reached the cache. The debugger logs full prompts, so it reached the audit log. The debtor memory profile keeps the last assembled record, so it reached the memory store.

That is one field and five retention surfaces, none of which are indexed by data subject. When the guarantor exercises the right to be forgotten, the honest answer is that you do not know where all the copies are.

The log is the worst of them, and for a reason that sounds like a paradox. Your SOC2 control says keep the audit trail seven years. GDPR says erase the personal data on request. Both are satisfiable at once — but only if the log never held the clear identifier in the first place.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing here was an attack or a bug. Each of the five copies was made by a component doing its documented job.
steps.youDo: Grep your own prompt logs for an SSN, EIN or card pattern. What comes back is your actual exposure, not your policy's.

terminal.text: where did the guarantor SSN end up?
trace_subject("412-88-7391", surfaces=["prompt","output","cache","log","memory"])
5 clear-text occurrences across 5 stores · 0 indexed by subject
erase("guarantor:ACME-88") -> UNSUPPORTED: no subject index on audit.log

cells: n/a — but it fed all four below
the summary quoted the guarantor line
the record sat inside the cached prefix
7 yrs — SOC2 says you may not delete it

view.text: Your retention control says keep the audit log for seven years. Your erasure obligation says delete this person's data on request. Those two are only compatible if the log never contained a clear identifier — which is a design decision you make before the first call, not a cleanup you run after the request arrives.

steps.title: Minimize first, tokenize what is left
narrative: Two controls, cheapest first. Minimize: keep the fields the risk task reads — filing IDs, secured parties, amounts, dates, status — and drop the other 27. Tokenize what must still be referenced: the SSN becomes tok_ssn_9f2c and the EIN becomes tok_ein_41ab, both resolvable only through a vault the model cannot call.
Then put a scanner between the assembler and the API. It runs on the assembled block before the send, and it fails closed: a clear identifier pattern in the block is a blocked call, not a warning.

The filing block drops from 3,200 tokens to 780 and the whole call from 5,540 to 3,120 — 44% cheaper. That is a side effect, not the point. The point is that the risk verdict is unchanged, because the guarantor's SSN was never an input to it.
steps.claudeSays: I scored the same five liens and returned the same verdict. The tokens I no longer see are the tokens that were never load-bearing.
steps.youDo: Add pii_scan(block) immediately before your API call and let it raise. A post-hoc log scrubber runs after the data has already left.

terminal.text: pii_scan(raw_block)
SSN pattern at offset 1,842 · DOB at offset 1,901 · street address at offset 2,110
⛔ clear PII in assembled block — call blocked before send
block = redact(filing, task="lien_risk")

dropped 27 fields the risk task never reads
SSN -> tok_ssn_9f2c   EIN -> tok_ein_41ab   (vault-resolved, out of band)
filing block: 3,200 -> 780 tokens

HIGH RISK — 5 active liens, $2.4M secured, 3 filed in the last 18 months.

steps.title: Log the access, not the secret
narrative: Minimization alone would leave you compliant and unable to prove it. The audit trail is the other half: for every call, record who acted, on whose data, for which tenant, when, which guardrails ran, and a SHA-256 of the assembled context — enough to reconstruct that a specific window was sent, without storing what was in it.

Now the erasure request is a five-second operation instead of an incident. Destroy tok_ssn_9f2c in the vault and every downstream reference — prompt, report, cache, memory — dereferences to nothing, because none of them ever held the value. The audit log survives untouched, which is what your retention control required.
That is the module's rule in one line: you cannot prove compliance you did not log, and you cannot erase a secret you logged. Log the access. Never the secret.
steps.claudeSays: The record of this call is 180 bytes of metadata and a hash. It proves the access happened and reveals nothing about the person.
steps.youDo: Write erase(subject_id) before you write the feature that stores personal data. If erasure is hard to write, your storage design is the thing that is wrong.

terminal.text: audit(actor="analyst:jrivera", tenant="lenderA", subject="debtor:ACME-FL-88")
audit event written · 0 clear identifiers · ctx_sha256 recorded
the guarantor has requested erasure. what has to go?
erase("guarantor:ACME-88")

vault: tok_ssn_9f2c destroyed
memory profile purged · 3 cache keys invalidated · report reference dereferenced
audit log retained in full (7-yr SOC2 control) — it never held a clear identifier

data.output: HIGH RISK — guarantor SSN 412-88-7391, 5 active liens ...

views.text: The same call, twice. The first version answers the regulator's question — what did you do, with whose data, when — and also hands them a breach. The second answers it and hands them nothing, because the only clear copy of the identifier lives in a vault with one door and a delete button.
